{{short description|Extinct Chimakuan language}} {{For|the community named Chimacum|Chimacum, Washington}} {{Infobox language | name = Chemakum | nativename = {{lang|xch|Aqoʞúlo}} | states = [[Olympic Peninsula]], [[Washington (state)|Washington]] | ethnicity = [[Chimakum]] | extinct = 1940s | ref = | familycolor = American | fam1 = [[Chimakuan languages|Chimakuan]] | iso3 = xch | glotto = chim1310 | glottorefname = Chimakum | linglist = xch | notice = IPA | pronunciation = /{{IPA|ʔaˈxʷóqʷolo}}/ }} '''Chemakum''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|tʃ|ɛ|m|ə|k|ʌ|m}} {{respell|CHEM|ək|um}}; also written as '''Chimakum''' or '''Chimacum''') is an extinct [[Chimakuan language]] once spoken by the [[Chemakum]], a [[Native Americans in the United States|Native American]] group that once lived on western [[Washington (state)|Washington]] state's [[Olympic Peninsula]]. It was closely related to the [[Quileute language]], also extinct but undergoing revitalization in the early 21st century. In the 1860s, [[Chief Seattle]] and the [[Suquamish people|Suquamish]] people killed many of the [[Chimakum]] people. In 1890, [[Franz Boas]] found out about only three speakers, and they spoke it imperfectly, of whom he managed to gather linguistic data from one, a woman named Louise Webster (her brother was another speaker of the three).{{cite book |last= Ruby |first= Robert H. |author2=John Arthur Brown |title= A Guide to the Indian Tribes of the Pacific Northwest |year= 1992 |publisher= University of Oklahoma Press |isbn= 9780806124797 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=-7zBc-pqnGsC&pg=PA22 |pages= 22–23, 28}} The name ''Chemakum'' is an anglicization of the [[Salishan languages|Salishan]] name for the Chimakum people, perhaps old [[Twana language|Twana]] {{lang|twa|čə́mqəm}} (currently {{lang|twa|čə́bqəb}} {{IPA|[t͡ʃə́bqəb]}}). ==Phonology== Boas’{{Cite journal |last=Boas |first=Franz |date=1892 |title=Notes on the Chemakum language |journal=American Anthropologist |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=37–44 |doi=10.1525/aa.1892.5.1.02a00050 |jstor=658768 |doi-access=free }} original article based on fieldwork with one of the last three native speakers in the summer of 1890 uses the following consonantal symbols: {{lang|xch|‹h; k, ʞ, q; u; y; n; t; s, c, tç; ts, tc; m, p; l, lʻ; ′›}} along with ejectivization usually notated by a following {{lang|xch|‹!›}} on stops and affricates, but sometimes also by a following {{lang|xch|‹ߴ›}}. Labio-dorsals and the lateral ejective were analyzed as consonant clusters as the transcription shows. Based on his own description (in a footnote) and words and sentences cited, along with some comparison to [http://quileutelanguage.com/quildict.html Quileute cognates], the following phonemic inventory can be determined (the plain uvulars were probably pre-uvular and the plain stops and affricates were probably somewhat aspirated as in most languages of the region including Quileute): {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" |- !rowspan="2" colspan="2"| !rowspan="2"|[[Bilabial consonant|Bilabial]] !colspan="3"|[[Alveolar consonant|Alveolar]] !rowspan="2"|[[Palato-alveolar consonant|Palato-

[[Affricate]] ! plain | {{IPA link|p}} ‹p› | {{IPA link|t}} ‹t› | {{IPA link|t͡s}} ‹ts› | | {{IPA link|t͡ʃ}} ‹tc› | {{IPA link|kʷ}} ‹ku› | {{IPA link|q}} ‹ʞ› | {{IPA link|qʷ}} ‹ʞu› | rowspan="2" | {{IPA link|ʔ}} ‹′› |- ![[Ejective consonant|ejective]] | {{IPA link|pʼ}} ‹p!› | {{IPA link|tʼ}} ‹t!› | {{IPA link|t͡sʼ}} ‹ts!› | {{IPA link|t͡ɬʼ}} ‹t!lʻ› | {{IPA link|t͡ʃʼ}} ‹tc!› | {{IPA link|kʷʼ}} ‹k!u› | {{IPA link|qʼ}} ‹ʞ!› | {{IPA link|qʷʼ}} ‹ʞ!u› |- ! colspan="2"| [[Fricative]] | | | {{IPA link|s}} ‹s› | {{IPA link|ɬ}} ‹lʻ› | {{IPA link|ʃ}} ‹c› | | {{IPA link|χ}} ‹q› | {{IPA link|χʷ}} ‹qu› | {{IPA link|h}} ‹h› |- ! colspan="2"| [[Sonorant]] | {{IPA link|m}} ‹m› | {{IPA link|n}} ‹n› | | {{IPA link|l}} ‹l› | {{IPA link|j}} ‹y› | {{IPA link|w}} ‹u› | | | |} Transcription is not fully standardized and some amount of variation is attested. For example, some instances of ejectives are double-marked with both ‹!› and a following ‹ߴ›. Compare the independent word ‘back’ written {{lang|xch|‹ʞ!ߴē′enōkoat›}} against the corresponding lexical suffix, written {{lang|xch|‹-ʞ!ĕnuk›}}. Similarly, the lexical suffix for ‘hand’ appears as {{lang|xch|‹-t!ߴa›}}. Here, the Quileute cognate {{lang|qui|‹-t̓ay›}} shows that, despite the notation, the sound was probably just an ejective ''t''. Yet another notation for an ejective – simply a following apostrophe – may be found in the word {{lang|xch|‹ʞ!ߴautߴátct›}}, perhaps ‘bracelet’, if this is indeed cognate to Quileute {{lang|qui|‹ḳ̓aḳ̓ʷò·t̓á·yat›}} ‘bracelet’; and in {{lang|xch|‹tcߴālʻa›}} ‘stone’, cognate to Quileute {{lang|qui|‹k̓á·t̓ƚa›}} ‘stone’. The labio-dorsals were not analyzed as unit consonants by Boas. The audible rounding on them was either marked as a glide, or the rounding was notationally transferred to a neighboring vowel. Consider the following examples: {{lang|xch|‹kuē′lʻ›}} ‘one’ (Quileute {{lang|qui|‹wí·ƚ›}}), {{lang|xch|‹lʻa′kua›}} ‘two’ (Quileute {{lang|qui|‹ƚáʔw›}}), {{lang|xch|‹ʞoā′lē›}} ‘three’ (Quileute {{lang|qui|‹ḳʷáʔl›}}), {{lang|xch|‹-kō›}} ‘canoe (lexical suffix)’ (Quileute {{lang|qui|‹-kʷ›}}), {{lang|xch|‹-ʞōs›}} ‘neck (lexical suffix)’ (Quileute {{lang|qui|‹-ḳ̓ʷó·s›}}), {{lang|xch|‹-tçuʞ›}} ‘our’ (Quileute {{lang|qui|‹-t̓oqʷ›}}) etc. The meaning of Boas’ {{lang|xch|‹tç›}} is not entirely certain. Swadesh,{{Cite journal |last=Swadesh |first=Morris |date=1955 |title=Chemakum lexicon compared with Quileute |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1263215 |journal=International Journal of American Linguistics |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=60–72 |doi=10.1086/464309 |jstor=1263215 |s2cid=143862109 |url-access=subscription }} working with Boas’ data half a century later, decided to interpret ‹tç› as {{IPA|/t͡ʃʼ/}} – in his notation {{lang|xch|‹ч̓›}} – but it is not clear why, especially considering that {{IPA|/t͡ʃʼ/}} is written differently in {{lang|xch|‹tcߴālʻa›}} ‘stone’. Boas himself describes the sound as “dento-alveolar t”, which is not very helpful. Based on comparative evidence from Quileute, Powell{{Cite book |last=Powell |first=James V. |title=Proto-Chimakuan: Materials for a Reconstruction |publisher=PhD dissertation at the University of Hawaiʻi |year=1974 |page=16}} interprets {{lang|xch|‹tç›}} as a variant symbol for {{IPA|/t/}} (perhaps notating some allophonic difference that Boas perceived). The list was reduced to a much simpler phonemic inventory of three short vowels {{IPA|/i a o/}} and three long vowels {{IPA|/iː aː oː/}} by Powell.{{Cite journal |last=Elmendorf |first=William W. |date=1990 |editor-last=Suttles |editor-first=Wayne |title=Chemakum |journal=Handbook of North American Indians |volume=7 |issue=Northwest Coast |pages=438–440}} The vowels probably exhibited some amount of allophonic variation as Boas’ original transcription shows, but according to Andrade,{{Cite journal |last=Andrade |first=Manuel J. |date=1933 |editor-last=Boas |editor-first=Franz |title=Quileute |journal=Handbook of Indian American Languages |volume=3 |page=151}} less so than in Quileute. ==See also== * [[Quileute language]] * [[Chimakuan languages]] == References == {{reflist}} {{Languages of the United States}} {{Indigenous peoples in Washington}} {{Authority control}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Chemakum Language}} [[Category:Chimakuan languages]] [[Category:Languages of the United States]] [[Category:Extinct languages of North America]] [[Category:Indigenous languages of Washington (state)]]
